title: Files, pages and records
lead: File organisation, fixed and variable-length pages, slotted pages and record representation.

sections.title: Database files and heap files
sections.html:
A logical database file is a collection of pages containing records. The file layer supports creating files, inserting/deleting/updating records, fetching a record by RID and scanning records. A logical file can span operating-system files or machines.

Heap files store records without a key order. They must track their pages, free space and record locations. One implementation maintains separate linked lists of full pages and pages with free space; searching for enough space may visit many pages.

A page directory stores page identifiers and free-space information in compact directory pages. A cached directory can locate a suitable data page with fewer reads. Sorted files and index-organised files offer other access/update trade-offs.

PDF pp. 1–9

sections.title: Fixed-length page layouts
sections.html:
A page header records metadata such as the page ID, record count and free space. With fixed-length packed records, position i starts at headerSize + (i − 1)·recordSize. Insertion appends after the current last record.

Deleting a packed record can fill its gap with the last record, but this changes that moved record’s position-based RID. Any references to that RID may need updating.

An unpacked layout leaves empty slots. A bitmap marks occupied positions, or a free list links available slots. Insertion reuses a free slot and deletion releases one, so unrelated records need not move. The layout trades metadata and unused space for stable positions.

PDF pp. 10–19

sections.title: Variable-length records and slotted pages
sections.html:
Variable-length records cannot be located using one constant record size. A slotted page instead maintains a directory mapping slot IDs to current record offsets. Its RID is (page ID, slot ID).

The slot directory and records grow from opposite parts of the page. Insertion uses an available slot or creates one and allocates enough bytes for the record. Deletion invalidates the slot; compaction can move remaining record bytes and update their directory offsets.

Moving bytes within a page does not change a record’s RID while its slot ID remains unchanged. This indirection allows compaction without rewriting external references to every moved record. Reusing a deleted slot still requires the DBMS’s normal record-lifecycle rules.

PDF pp. 20–23

sections.title: Record layout and NULL representation
sections.html:
Field types belong to the schema stored in the system catalog, so each record need not repeat its complete schema. Fixed-length fields can be addressed by offsets computed from the field sizes.

Variable-length fields can use delimiters or an offset array. Delimiters require scanning and escaping; offsets support direct field access. Another layout keeps fixed-size offset/length descriptors near fixed-length values and stores variable data afterwards.

NULL requires explicit metadata, commonly a bitmap. An empty variable-length field and a NULL field cannot always be distinguished by offsets alone. The source’s byte-layout figure combines numeric fields, string descriptors, string bytes and a NULL bitmap.

PDF pp. 24–29

quiz.question: In the slotted-page example, must the index change the RID when the record in slot 2 moves?
options: No, if the slot ID remains unchanged
The RID is a byte offset, so the record cannot move
quiz.explanation: The slot directory updates the byte offset. The index still finds the record through (page 9, slot 2).
